learningObjective: Distinguish dynamic (request-level) batching from continuous (iteration-level) batching and diagnose a workload that suffers head-of-line blocking.
stem: A serving stack uses dynamic batching (each 'batch' completes fully before the next batch starts). The following aggregated metrics are observed for a workload with heterogeneous output lengths. What is the correct diagnosis?
profileData:
Server: 8 concurrent requests batched per iteration.
  Output length distribution across a batch: 15, 20, 22, 28, 30, 35, 800, 40 tokens.
  Observed metrics (per batch):
    - GPU utilization during first 40 decode steps: ~78%
    - GPU utilization during decode steps 41 through 800: ~13%
    - Wall time: 800 * ~20 ms = ~16 s
    - Requests 1-7 (short) block waiting for request 8 to complete before returning.
    - New arriving requests wait for the batch to finish before being scheduled.

options.text: This is head-of-line blocking under request-level (static) dynamic batching: the batch is dominated by the single long request, wasting SM cycles on almost-empty batches and delaying shorter requests. The right fix is to move to continuous (iteration-level) batching so shorter requests can leave the batch and new requests can join per iteration.
The workload is memory-bound during long decode; the correct fix is to enable KV cache quantization to speed up decode steps 41-800, which will bring GPU utilization back up.
The bottleneck is compute-bound decode; adding a smaller draft model for speculative decoding will improve utilization by generating multiple tokens per verification step.
This is a launch-overhead problem: 800 kernel launches per decode step create CPU-side dispatch gaps. The correct fix is CUDA Graph capture of the decode loop.

explanation: The signature is textbook static-batching head-of-line blocking: after the first ~40 decode steps, only one request (the 800-token one) remains active, but the batched kernel still runs at effective batch size 1, wasting SM parallelism. All shorter requests are held in the batch until the longest finishes; new requests cannot enter until the whole batch completes. Continuous (iteration-level) batching — Orca's contribution and vLLM's core scheduler — fixes exactly this by allowing per-iteration join/leave.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: HoL blocking under static batching, fixed by continuous batching.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: KV quantization does not address the batch composition problem.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: decode is memory-bound at batch-1; spec decoding helps but does not solve the imbalance.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: launch overhead is not the primary cause; the batch is running one long generation.

assumptions: The reported utilization measure captures effective batch size after short requests are done.
The scheduler is truly static (no per-iteration rebatching).
nonImplications: Does not imply KV quantization or CUDA Graphs are never useful; they are orthogonal levers.
Does not imply continuous batching solves all imbalance; extreme variance still requires additional policies (preemption, chunked prefill).

performanceClaim.scope: Head-of-line blocking diagnosis under static batching
